title: Jeffries Pledges Early Action on Bill Protecting Children of H-1B Workers
excerpt: The American Dream and Promise Act, which covers documented Dreamers who age out at 21, is one signature short of a forced House vote — and its Democratic leader says it moves early next Congress if it stalls now.
body:
• House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries pledged on Wednesday to move the American Dream and Promise Act early in the next Congress if it does not pass in this one.
  • The bill, H.R. 1589, expressly covers eligible sons and daughters of H-1B, L-1, E-1 and E-2 visa holders — the "documented Dreamers" who age out of dependent status at 21.
  • A discharge petition to force a House floor vote stands at 217 signatures, one short of the 218 needed; every House Democrat has signed, so the deciding signature must come from a Republican or the chamber's independent member.
  • Nothing can be filed yet — the bill is not law. What families can do now: check whether their representative has signed the petition, and know the bill dies when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 unless it passes both chambers and is signed.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday pledged to advance immigration legislation that could offer permanent residency to eligible children of Indian H-1B workers, saying Congress should act immediately or Democrats would take it up early in the next Congress, IANS reported from Washington.

"I can guarantee you that if that doesn't happen, we're going to move the Dream and Promise Act in the next Congress, early in the next Congress," Jeffries told reporters at a news conference. He described the bill as a starting point for wider changes: "We should start with the Dream and Promise Act, but that's the beginning. That's not the end." Asked whether he had spoken to President Donald Trump about an immigration agreement, Jeffries said: "Haven't heard from the President yet."

Who is covered — and who is not

The American Dream and Promise Act of 2025 (H.R. 1589) would create a path to permanent residence for people brought to the United States as children. For Indian families, the significant provision is Section 102, which expressly includes anyone who "is the son or daughter of an alien admitted as a nonimmigrant" under the E-1, E-2, H-1B or L-1 categories, according to an analysis of the bill text by the immigration law firm Reddy Neumann Brown PC. Children of E-3, H-1B1, O-1, R-1 and TN workers are not expressly included in that provision.

These young people are known as "documented Dreamers": they grew up legally in the United States as dependents of temporary visa holders, but because of decades-long employment-based green card backlogs — particularly large for people born in India and China, the American Immigration Council notes — many lose their dependent status when they turn 21. Those who cannot obtain another lawful status may have to leave despite having spent much of their childhood in the country.

Two drafting points widen the bill's reach. It uses "son or daughter" rather than "child," so there is no maximum age at application — someone who has already aged out of H-4 status can still qualify. And it does not expressly require applicants to still hold dependent status, so a person who switched to an F-1 student visa, or had a lapse in status after turning 21, could still be eligible if they meet the other requirements.

Scope of the coverage: counted here are sons and daughters of E-1, E-2, H-1B and L-1 nonimmigrants who entered the US at 18 or younger. Not counted are children of E-3, H-1B1, O-1, R-1 and TN workers, who are not named in the documented Dreamer provision.

What the bill would actually grant

Eligible applicants would receive lawful permanent residence on a conditional basis for 10 years, IANS reported. Conditions can be removed by completing qualifying higher education, serving at least two years in the Uniformed Services, or demonstrating earned income over a qualifying period; some applicants who already meet the removal requirements at application — including the English and civics standard — could receive permanent residence without conditions from the outset. Section 305 exempts these green cards from annual numerical caps, which is the core benefit for Indian-born families facing the longest waits, and Section 311 leaves other immigration routes open rather than forfeiting a pending family- or employment-based case.

Where it stands: one signature short

H.R. 1589 was introduced on February 26, 2025 by Representative Sylvia Garcia of Texas and has 221 cosponsors. After it stalled in committee, Garcia filed Discharge Petition No. 25 on July 20, 2026 to force it toward a floor vote. The petition has 217 signatures on the House Clerk's published tally — every House Democrat plus three Republicans: Representatives María Elvira Salazar, Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon. Reaching 218 would not trigger an immediate vote; the motion must sit on the discharge calendar for seven legislative days before it can be offered, and discharge motions are not in order during the last six days of a session.

"I can guarantee you that if that doesn't happen, we're going to move the Dream and Promise Act in the next Congress, early in the next Congress."

— Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic Leader

What to do now

There is no application to file and no fee to pay — the bill is not law, and approval by both chambers plus a presidential signature would be required before any family could obtain relief. The clock is real: if the measure is not enacted before the current Congress ends in January 2027, it must be reintroduced and begin the legislative process again, and the discharge petition expires with it.

The one action available today is political. You do not need to be a US citizen to contact a congressional office. Find your representative via house.gov, check the petition tally in the IANS report and the bill analysis from Reddy Neumann Brown PC, and — because every Democrat has already signed — a call matters most if your representative is a Republican or the House's independent member. Background on who documented Dreamers are is in the American Immigration Council's fact sheet.
